A: Chapter 2 opens the teaching. 2.1–10 (frame): Kṛṣṇa rebukes Arjuna's faintness and unmanliness (2.2–3); Arjuna restates his dilemma — he cannot fight Bhīṣma and Droṇa, would rather live on alms, does not know which outcome is better — and asks Kṛṣṇa, as his disciple who has come for refuge, to tell him for certain what is better (śreyas) (2.4–8); he says 'I will not fight' and falls silent, and Kṛṣṇa, as if smiling, answers (2.9–10). 2.11–30: the teaching on the embodied self (dehin): the wise do not grieve; the self was never not and will never cease; it passes through bodies as through the ages of life and as through garments; the unreal has no being and the real no non-being; the self neither slays nor is slain, is unborn, eternal, uncuttable, unmanifest and unthinkable; even on the contrary view birth and death are inevitable; therefore do not grieve. 2.31–38: the argument from one's own dharma (svadharma) and honour: a dharmic battle is the kṣatriya's best good and a door to heaven, refusal brings sin and disgrace; fight treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike. 2.39: transition — the understanding (buddhi) given 'in sāṃkhya' is now given 'in yoga'. 2.40–53: the yoga of understanding (buddhi-yoga): resolute understanding is one (2.41); the flowery speech of those who delight in Vedic statements and seek heaven and power keeps understanding from samādhi; the Vedas concern the three guṇas, be free of them (2.42–46); your right is to action, not its fruits; yoga is sameness and skill in actions; the wise, yoked with understanding, abandon the fruit and are freed from the bondage of birth (2.47–51); when understanding passes beyond delusion and stands steady in samādhi, you will attain yoga (2.52–53). 2.54–72: Arjuna asks about the person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña); Kṛṣṇa describes him: he gives up all desires and is content in the self, unshaken by sorrow and pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger, withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.55–61); the chain from dwelling on objects through attachment, desire, anger, delusion and loss of memory to ruin (2.62–63), and its reverse through mastered senses to serenity and steady understanding (2.64–68); the sage is awake where beings sleep, is filled by desires like the ocean yet unmoved, and without 'mine' and 'I' attains peace (2.69–71); this is the brahmic state, reaching which even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72). The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to answer Arjuna's grief and his request for the good, first by knowledge of the self, then by the discipline of action done with steady understanding, culminating in the portrait of the one whose wisdom is steady.
B: Chapter 2 (72 verses) begins the teaching. 2.1–10: Kṛṣṇa rebukes Arjuna's faintness of heart (2.2–3); Arjuna restates his dilemma about fighting his revered elders, declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple who has taken refuge and asks what is better (2.4–8), then says he will not fight (2.9); Kṛṣṇa, as if smiling, replies (2.10). 2.11–30: the argument from the embodied one (dehin): the wise do not grieve; neither Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna nor the kings ever were not or will not be; the embodied one passes through bodies as through the ages of life and as one changes clothes; the unreal has no being and the real no non-being; the embodied one is indestructible, unborn, eternal, neither slays nor is slain, cannot be cut, burnt, wetted or dried, is unmanifest and unthinkable — so grief is misplaced; even if it were born and died again and again, death is certain for the born, and grief would still be unfit (2.26–28). 2.31–38: the argument from Arjuna's own dharma (svadharma) and honour: a battle in accordance with dharma is the best thing for a kṣatriya and an open door to heaven; refusing brings sin and disgrace; fight with pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat made the same. 2.39–53: the same understanding (buddhi) 'according to yoga': no effort is lost; resolute understanding is one; those who delight in Vedic words aimed at heaven and power lack it; the Vedas deal with the three guṇas — be beyond them; the entitlement is to action, not its fruits; yoga is equanimity (samatva) and skill in actions; the wise, abandoning the fruit, are freed from the bondage of birth; understanding immovable in samādhi attains yoga. 2.54–72: Arjuna asks about the one of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña); Kṛṣṇa describes him: free of desires, content in the self, unshaken by pain and pleasure, withdrawing the senses like a tortoise; the fall from dwelling on objects through attachment, desire, anger and delusion to ruin (2.62–63), and the rise through senses free of passion and aversion to serenity (prasāda), steady understanding and peace (2.64–66); the sage awake in the night of beings; peace like the ocean receiving the rivers; the brāhmī sthiti, which, held even at death, attains brahmanirvāṇa.

A: Chapter 3 answers the question of understanding versus action. 3.1–2: Arjuna asks why, if understanding (buddhi) is held superior to action, Kṛṣṇa urges him to terrible action, and asks for one decisive teaching. 3.3–9: Kṛṣṇa says he declared of old a twofold commitment (niṣṭhā) — the yoga of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and the yoga of action for the yogins; actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) is not reached by not acting nor perfection by mere renunciation; no one can stay without acting, since the guṇas of prakṛti make everyone act; restraining the organs of action while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy, while karma-yoga with the senses controlled and without attachment excels; do your allotted action, for the world is bound by action except action for sacrifice. 3.10–16: Prajāpati created beings with sacrifice, telling them to nourish the gods and be nourished; who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief; eating the remains of sacrifice frees from fault; the wheel of food, rain, sacrifice, action, brahman and the imperishable must be kept turning. 3.17–18: for one who delights and is content in the self there is nothing that must be done. 3.19–26: therefore act unattached; Janaka and others reached perfection by action; act for the holding together of the world (loka-saṃgraha), since people follow the best; Kṛṣṇa himself, needing nothing, keeps acting lest the worlds perish; the wise should act unattached as the unwise act attached, and not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant. 3.27–29: actions are done by the guṇas, and only the ego-deluded thinks 'I am the doer'; the knower of the truth is not attached. 3.30–32: resign all actions to Kṛṣṇa and fight; those who follow this teaching with faith are released, those who cavil are lost. 3.33–35: all beings follow their nature; attraction and aversion lie in wait in the sense-objects; one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's. 3.36–43: Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will; Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger, born of rajas, the enemy that covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, seated in the senses, mind and understanding; restrain the senses first, know what is beyond understanding, steady the self by the self and slay desire. The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to show why Arjuna must act — action being unavoidable, sacrificial, exemplary and non-binding when done without attachment — and to name desire as what must be overcome.
B: Chapter 3 (43 verses) answers Arjuna's question why, if understanding is superior, he is urged to act. 3.1–2: Arjuna asks for the one thing that leads to the good. 3.3–9: Kṛṣṇa names two commitments (niṣṭhā) — jñānayoga for the Sāṃkhyas, karmayoga for the Yogins; freedom from action does not come by not acting nor perfection by mere renunciation; no one can remain without acting, since the guṇas of prakṛti make all act; restraining the organs of action while dwelling on objects in the mind is hypocrisy; one who acts with the organs of action, the senses controlled, unattached, excels; do prescribed action; action other than for sacrifice binds, so act for sacrifice without attachment. 3.10–16: the wheel of sacrifice: Prajāpati created beings with sacrifice; gods and humans nourish one another; one who enjoys without offering is a thief; eating the remainder of sacrifice frees from faults; beings–food–rain–sacrifice–action–brahman–the imperishable; one who does not turn the wheel lives in vain. 3.17–19: for one content in the self nothing remains to be done; therefore act unattached and attain the highest. 3.20–26: holding the world together (lokasaṃgraha): Janaka and others reached perfection by action; the best person sets the standard; Kṛṣṇa, who has nothing to attain, still acts lest the worlds perish; the knower should act unattached as the ignorant act attached, without unsettling their understanding. 3.27–29: the guṇas act; the one deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks 'I am the doer'; the knower of the truth is unattached. 3.30–32: renounce all actions in Kṛṣṇa and fight; those who follow this teaching with faith are freed, those who carp are lost. 3.33–35: beings follow their nature; passion and aversion in the senses are waylayers; one's own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's. 3.36–43: asked what drives a person to sin against his will, Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger, born of rajas, the enemy that covers knowledge and is seated in the senses, mind and understanding; control the senses first, know what is beyond the understanding, and slay desire.
